title: Ummon's Medicine and Sickness Correspond to Each Other
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny takes up Case 87 of the Blue Cliff Record, Yunmen's line "Medicine and disease correspond with each other. The whole world is medicine. Where do you find yourself?" Reizan traces the saying to the Avatamsaka Sutra, where Manjushri sends Sudhana to find something that is not medicine, and Sudhana comes back holding a blade of grass. Reizan then describes yelling at Brian Kilmeade on television during a week of fires and floods, and asks whether Yantou's great roar, paired with "Although he's young, he's capable," offers a way to meet that anger. The pandemic becomes disease and medicine at once, and Reizan closes by opening the floor so each person can say where they find themselves.

sentences.text: **Reizan Bob Penny:** Good evening everyone.
I'm going to give a talk tonight.
I guess it's centered on case 87 of the Blue Cliff Record.
Can everyone hear?
Just to be sure.
Good.
Master Yunmen Wen, who lived from 864 to 949, said, "Medicine and disease correspond with each other.
The whole world is medicine.
Where do you find yourself?"
It's also been translated in various ways: medicine and disease subdue each other, medicine and disease heal each other, are in accord with each other.
And instead of "Where do you find yourself?", "Who are you?"
All of these could be true, but I prefer the word "correspond" and I prefer the location in space.
The whole world is medicine.
Where do you find yourself?
This saying that Yunmen is using comes from the Avatamsaka Sutra.
There's a story in this long, expansive sutra from India.
Sudhana says to Manjushri, the Bodhisattva who wields the double-edged sword that cuts down ignorance and duality, "I want to resolve suffering."
And Manjushri says, "Go talk to 53 people."
So he does.
Sudhana goes and talks to all sorts of different people from many different walks of life and tries to find a resolve, a cure for suffering.
He comes back and says to Manjushri, "I'm still suffering."
So Manjushri says, "Show me something that's not medicine.
Go talk to 53 people again and try to find something that's not medicine."
So Sudhana talks to the 53 people again and comes back and is not able to find anything that is not medicine.
So Manjushri says, "Show me some medicine."
And Sudhana picks up a blade of grass.
And Manjushri says, "This blade of grass can kill someone or bring someone to life."
The Avatamsaka Sutra, the Flower Garland Sutra, is sort of the core text of the Huayan school of Buddhism.

It's the text that includes the well-known story about Indra's net, the net of jewels that reflects each and every thing in the world, reflected in each and every other thing in the world, infinitely.
It was taught to Princess Mu by one of the great masters, who set up a bunch of mirrors and lit a candle in the middle to show the infinite progression of reflections on into infinity.

I saw a nice little definition of the Huayan school in Wikipedia: *Huayan thought exists as distinct against the notion of cause and effect, asserting that all phenomenon exists in mutual interpenetration with all other phenomenon, only as a part of the total nexus of reality.* This Huayan philosophy has gained a lot more traction in the 20th century and probably underpins a lot of Buddhism's reputation as being an ecologically based philosophy or religion.
Yunmen was an heir to Zui Feng.
And Zui Feng got his great enlightenment while holed up in a cabin in a snowstorm with his great Dharma pal, Yan Tao.

Zui Feng's breakthrough happened after a long argument about whether it was better to meditate or sleep through the snowstorm, when Yan Tao said, "If you want to expound a great teaching, then it must flow from your own breast."

Yan Tao's own attainment was attested to by yet another master of the same century, Jian Shan, in a manner that brought up again the two-edged sword of giving and receiving life, medicine and illness.
Jian Shan was heir to De Cheng, the boat monk mentioned in the Mountains and Rivers Sutra.
There were a lot of these monks living in the 9th century, well aware of each other.
De Cheng pushed Jian Shan into the water.
When he crawled out, De Cheng said, "If you drop in a hook, you'll catch a golden fish," and Jian Shan was enlightened.
Of Jian Shan's encounter with De Cheng, Dogen four centuries later wrote, *Is it not catching a fish, catching a person, catching water, or catching the self?*
So, Jian Shan playfully wanted once to test Yan Tao and another teacher, Xishuang.
Once, Jian Shan sent a monk to Xishuang's temple.
The monk stood at the gate and said, "I don't understand."
Xishuang said, "Your reverence, there's no need."
The monk then said, "In that case, I'll say farewell."
The monk then went to Yan Tao's temple.
Acting as before, he said, "I don't understand."
Yan Tao gave out a great roar.
The monk said, "In that case, I'll say farewell."
Yan Tao said, "Although he's young, he's capable."
The monk went back and reported to Jian Shan, and Jian Shan brought the monk in front of the assembly.
They recounted the story and Jian Shan said, "Although Xishuang has the knife that kills, he doesn't have the sword that gives life."
Yan Tao has the knife that kills as well as the sword that gives life.

So, Yunmen came to this teaching that's in the Blue Cliff Record here from the Avatamsaka Sutra, through his teachers Wei Feng, who got something from his Dharma brother Yan Tao, as confirmed by Jian Shan, each teaching the other.
The whole world is medicine.
Where do you find yourself?
Well, yesterday I found myself yelling at the screen, at Brian Kilmeade of Fox and Friends.
No, it's not about a personal opinion or choice.
It's about personal responsibility.
I was yelling.
Kilmeade is animated and sure of himself, even as the world burns around him and democracy crumbles under the guise of people just exercising, quote unquote, freedom.
This week especially, I've been watching the fires and the floods, the literally biblical revelations that daily now unfold in our world as the evening news.
I look out my window and I see the leaves on the trees shriveling.
Certainly Kilmeade's personal choice, quote unquote, is odious in the face of the world's obvious current suffering.
Where's the sense of responsibility?
And then I thought, personal responsibility?
Responsibility implies something or someone beyond the self.
It's not actually describable as just personal.
The whole world is medicine, because all phenomenon exists in interpenetration with all other phenomenon.
Responsibility needs an object.
In fact, the whole world is medicine.
"Medicine and disease correspond" could as easily be restated as "the whole world is disease."
In other words, when the whole world is disease, that is a pandemic.
The pandemic has certainly shown that the whole world is struggling with the great pandemic of delusion, craving and aversion.

The whole world presents the disease of our delusion as medicine at every moment, each particle of ignorance or blindness offering perfect opportunities in every passing moment to catch a golden fish.
Suddenly, I could dial back my anger and discuss with Brian Kilmeade a little bitty bit.
I mean, yeah, I'm still angry about the blind, crazy death cult that has us in its grips and is driving our whole society in this world into oblivion.
Yeah, I'm mad about that.
But how much can I blame a person who is centered on what they seem to believe, trying to assert something he thinks is helpful, even if it's not?
Can I be Yan Tao offering a great roar, but also saying he's capable?
Do I see ignorance as clear evidence of potential for wisdom?
Do I see the whole world as medicine, ready to offer up something to heal every disease?
Certainly, the disease of COVID won't rest until it has taught the Brian Kilmeades of this world a thing or two about compassion and wisdom.
Maybe a disease like this is the medicine people like that need.
Medicine and disease correspond.
I can't remember seeing our world, our whole world, in such a place as this before.
We're all in the grip of one basic issue.
Will we help each other in this world?
Will we heal the disease of our time, the heating of the entire planet into a chaotic dysfunction of climate imbalance?
The loss of compassionate responsiveness has evolved into a disease.
The whole world is offering medicine, even if it's the kind of medicine one must suffer through, like the vaccine producing a war of antibodies inside us.
Like the chemotherapy of global warming, burning out the cancer but hurting us as it does.
In this place, medicine is often tough to take.
And we are in very difficult times where the way forward looks dangerous on all sides.
But can we see how the whole world heals itself?
How nature always works towards balance?
We just have to position our own efforts to best help, to find ourselves somewhere where ills and cures may correspond.

So, Master Yuanwu, the compiler of the Blue Cliff Record, says about this case 87 in his pointer, which is an introductory statement that in these kinds of texts usually seems pretty confusing, but maybe here we can see something.
He says, *A clear-eyed person has no rest, has no nest, sorry, a clear-eyed person has no nest.*
*Sometimes on the summit of a solitary peak weeds grow in profusion.
Sometimes they're naked and free in the bustling marketplace.
Suddenly they appear as an angry Titan with three heads and six arms.
Suddenly a sun-face or moon-face Buddha.
They release the light of an all-embracing mercy.
In a single atom, they manifest all the physical forms to save people according to their type.
They mix with mud and water.
If suddenly they release an opening upwards, not even the Buddha's eyes can see them.
Even if a thousand sages appeared, they would have to fall back 3000 miles.
Is there anyone with the same attainment and the same realization?
To test this, I cite this old case.*
*Yunmen, teaching his community, said, "Medicine and disease correspond.
The whole world is medicine.
Where do you find yourself?"*
I have a feeling, at least for myself, that this is a powerful question.
Where do I find myself right now?
And I'm wondering if perhaps others are thinking of that question too.
And so I thought maybe we would open the floor, allow a little discussion.
People can reflect on this moment of disease that the world is experiencing, that we're experiencing, and where we find ourselves.
Where do you find yourself?
So I invite people to speak in your own turn.
**Participant:** Thank you, Bob, for this insightful talk.
I like the way you linked the medicine for the whole world.
When there's nothing that's not medicine, then the disease is medicine too.
And that is something that just goes against intuition and everything, especially in this time of COVID-19.
And yet it has been very revealing what is truly going on in the world, especially with groups and people outside of my bubble.
And just for myself, the world is very different from the way I thought four or five years ago.
So your koan exploration is great food for thought.
Thank you very much.
